extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners in biotechnology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a specification shows possession of the claimed invention under the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, with emphasis on biological subject matter (proteins, nucleic acids, alleles, variants, and bioinformatics methods). Contains examples and practice notes for examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must demonstrate that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing (satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the disclosure, alone or combined with knowledge in the art, conveys to one of ordinary skill that the inventor possessed the full scope of the claimed subject matter. Use representative species, common structural attributes, correlation between structure and function, or adequate descriptive detail to show possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial protein structure plus identifying characteristics can suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial protein structure (e.g., a short N‑terminal amino acid sequence) combined with other identifying characteristics (ability to bind/activate a target, approximate molecular weight, purification/isolation method, HPLC elution fraction, etc.) and a working isolation example may show possession of the claimed protein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating protein claims that lack full sequence disclosure, consider (1) the partial structural disclosure, (2) other identifying characteristics, and (3) whether a working isolation method is disclosed and exemplified. If these together would enable a skilled artisan to recognize the inventor had possession of the claimed protein, written description may be satisfied (see In re Wallach style fact pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: DNA claims based solely on partial protein information are generally inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of only partial protein sequence and identifying protein characteristics (without DNA sequence, deposit, or cloned DNA) generally fails to provide possession of the full scope of claimed DNAs that encode the protein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many different DNAs can encode the same partial amino acid sequence (genetic code degeneracy) and the remainder of the DNA sequence is unpredictable, scholars should require disclosure of at least one DNA species or other identifying attributes sufficient to represent the claimed DNA genus. Prophetic examples for making DNA libraries are not dispositive where unpredictability exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete sequence disclosure supports claims to that nucleic acid species
rubrics_metrics.description: When the specification discloses the complete chemical structure (e.g., SEQ ID NO: 1) of a nucleic acid and demonstrates reduction to practice, the specification can satisfy the written description requirement for a claim to that nucleic acid species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim directed to a particular isolated nucleic acid sequence is supported when the sequence is fully disclosed even if no deposit is made — possession is shown by the complete sequence and exemplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims defined by hybridization under stringent conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to nucleic acids that hybridize under highly stringent conditions to a complement of a disclosed sequence may be supported by the disclosure of that sequence plus an explicit definition of highly stringent hybridization conditions and the well‑known behavior of hybridization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because highly stringent hybridization requires high structural similarity, disclosure of a species sequence plus defined stringent conditions and knowledge in the art may place one in possession of the genus of sequences that would hybridize under those conditions. However, if the genus is further limited by function (e.g., encode a protein having a function) and no correlation between structure and function is provided, support may still fail for the function‑limited genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad functional genus claims require representative species or correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to a broad genus defined only by function (e.g., 'isolated nucleic acids that encode a protein that binds to receptor X') are not supported by disclosure of a single species unless the specification or the art provides a correlation (structural or domain) that makes the single species representative of the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate predictability and common structural features across the claimed genus. If receptor‑binding domains or common sequence motifs are known or disclosed such that a single species is representative, support may exist. If the proteins/nucleic acids can vary substantially and no common attributes or correlations are disclosed, the specification likely fails to show possession of the entire genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allelic variant claims require more than a single allele disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that discloses only one allele sequence is generally insufficient to support claims to a broader genus of allelic variants (native alleles) because alleles are variant and unpredictable without disclosure of mutational sites or common attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless the specification describes how known allelic variation relates structurally or functionally to the disclosed allele (or provides representative alleles), applicants should not be treated as having been in possession of the full allelic genus. The ordinary meaning of 'allele' and supporting authority may be used to interpret scope; the Office should cite references when relying on term interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative number / common structural attributes requirement for genus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To support a genus claim, the specification must either disclose a representative number of species or describe common structural features that identify the genus; the number of species required rises with the degree of variability in the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the genus is highly variable (many different possible structures/functions), a single species disclosure is less likely to be representative. Examiner should assess predictability in the art and whether common attributes are taught that unify the claimed genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic examples are weak evidence when unpredictability exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic examples (e.g., proposed methods for making a library of DNAs) may not establish possession of claimed species or genus where the art is unpredictable; prophetic procedures that might eventually produce a species do not show possession at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on prophetic examples to support broad claims in unpredictable arts (e.g., isolating unknown DNA species). Consider whether the prophetic method is routine and predictable in the field; if not, written description support is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of general knowledge in the art to supplement disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: General, well‑known correlations or knowledge in the art (e.g., the genetic code's degeneracy, routine methods for protein modification, or standard bioinformatics practices) may supplement the specification to show possession of some claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether knowledge in the art would allow skilled artisans to envision the claimed genus or species from the disclosure. Examples: genetic code allows predicting degenerately related DNAs encoding a disclosed protein; routine fusion protein methods may justify genus claims defined by additions/fusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to highly variant product families (unlimited substitutions/deletions/insertions) often fail
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting variants generically (one or more amino acid substitutions, deletions, insertions, additions) without bounds or exemplified representative variants often fails written description when the genus is highly variant and no common identifying attributes are disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When variant scope is open‑ended and a representative number of species or common attributes are not disclosed, enter a written description rejection for the unsupported scope. Fusion/addition variants may be more predictable and supported, but substitution/deletion/insertion variants usually require more description.

rubrics_metrics.name: High‑identity variant claims (e.g., ≥95% identity) can be supported by a single sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to variants defined by a high percent sequence identity to a disclosed sequence (for example, at least 95% identical to SEQ ID NO: 3) can be supported by disclosure of that sequence because the high‑identity limitation identifies a concrete partial structure common to the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed identity threshold and the disclosure enable one skilled in the art to identify and make sequences with the claimed identity. High percent identity narrows the genus and may render a single disclosed sequence representative; however, if function is additionally required and no guidance which residues can vary while retaining function is given, support for the function‑limited genus may still fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product‑by‑function claims need structure‑function correlation or descriptive guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a product by its function (e.g., 'variant that catalyzes reaction A->B') require disclosure of which structural features are responsible for the function or sufficient descriptive guidance to show possession of variants that perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification discloses only one species with the function and does not teach which portions of the structure can vary while retaining function, a broader claim to variants that have the function may be unsupported. Examiner should require correlation or representative examples showing which changes preserve function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bioinformatics/computer‑implemented method claims can be supported by method steps plus ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer‑implemented method that recites steps (e.g., analyzing expression, inputting data, displaying axes and marks, selecting compounds based on plotted positions) may satisfy written description even if the specification does not disclose particular algorithms, devices, or example data, provided the steps and required physical steps are sufficiently described and the art makes their implementation routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the specification teaches the steps of the claimed method and whether implementation is routine for one skilled in the art. If so, possession of the claimed method may be found despite the absence of detailed algorithms or exemplified data. Consider cited case law on programming microprocessors and routine implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office burden to cite authority for claim term interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Office relies on a particular technical or ordinary meaning of a claim term (e.g., 'allele'), it should support that interpretation with citations to authoritative sources (practice note referencing MPEP 2163.04).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should cite authoritative glossaries, treatises, or case law when using such references to construe claim scope for written description analysis. This practice strengthens the Office's position and clarifies claim interpretation for applicants.
